draft.title: Circumference of a circle
card: The circumference is the distance around a circle. For every circle, the circumference divided by the diameter is the same number. That number is pi, written \(\pi\).
Pi is a little more than 3. We use \(\pi \approx 3.14\), or the \(\pi\) button on a calculator for a more exact answer.
\(C = \pi \times d\). The diameter is the width of the circle through its centre.
\(C = 2 \times \pi \times r\). The radius is half the diameter, so double it first. Example: for \(r = 5\) cm, \(C = 2 \times \pi \times 5 = 10\pi \approx 31.4\) cm.
draft.remember: Circumference is \(\pi\) times the diameter, or \(2\) times \(\pi\) times the radius.

a.q: A round pond has a diameter of 10 m. Using \(\pi \approx 3.14\), what is its circumference?
a.why: Use \(C = \pi \times d\), so \(C = 3.14 \times 10 = 31.4\) m. The answer 62.8 m comes from doubling the diameter as if it were a radius.
a.clue: The diameter is given, so use it directly.

b.q: A round clock has a radius of 20 cm. Ribbon is wrapped once around its edge. Using \(\pi \approx 3.14\), how much ribbon is needed?
b.why: Use \(C = 2 \times \pi \times r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 20 = 125.6\) cm. The answer 62.8 cm comes from using \(\pi \times r\), which skips the doubling.
b.clue: The distance around the edge is the circumference. Is 20 cm the radius or the diameter?

problems.detail: The card defines diameter ('the width of the circle through its centre') and explains the radius as half the diameter. These belong to point 2 (Parts of a circle), so here they should only be mentioned, not defined.

check.summary: Both questions and their explanations are correct (31.4 m and 125.6 cm). The only issue is that the card defines diameter and radius, which belong to the Parts of a circle point.
